name: Chamseddine-Volkov Monopole
description: A static, spherically symmetric monopole of gauged supergravity in four dimensions, with a Yang-Mills field, a dilaton, and no Higgs field, regular everywhere and supersymmetric. Its plane of time and radius is conformal to half of the flat plane, so its causal structure is that of Minkowski space, although it is not asymptotically flat.
convention: We use Chamseddine and Volkov's units, $c = 4\pi G = 1$ with the gauge coupling $1$, in which the scale $a$ is a length, and turn their signature $(+,-,-,-)$ to $(-,+,+,+)$ [chamseddine1997]. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A magnetic monopole can be made of a Yang-Mills field, a dilaton, and gravity, with no Higgs field [chamseddine1997]. Ali H. Chamseddine of ETH Zürich and Mikhail S. Volkov of the University of Zürich found it in 1997 among the supersymmetric solutions of an $N = 4$ supergravity [chamseddine1997]. Daniel Z. Freedman and John H. Schwarz had built that theory, with gauge group $SU(2) \times SU(2)$, in 1978 [freedman1978]. Chamseddine and Volkov kept one of its two Yang-Mills fields, purely magnetic, together with gravity and the dilaton, whose potential acts as "an effective negative, position-dependent cosmological term" [chamseddine1997]. Solving the conditions for supersymmetry to survive, Chamseddine and Volkov found in closed form all the static, spherically symmetric, purely magnetic supersymmetric solutions of the truncated theory [chamseddine1997]. They showed in 1998 that with both Yang-Mills fields present no such solution exists, and that the solutions they had found keep a quarter of the supersymmetries [chamseddine1998].¶One of these solutions is regular everywhere, with line element $ds^2 = a^2 (\sinh\rho / R)(-dt^2 + d\rho^2 + R^2 d\Omega^2)$, where $R^2 = 2\rho\coth\rho - \rho^2/\sinh^2\rho - 1$ and $a$ is a free scale [chamseddine1997]. Its Yang-Mills field has the amplitude $w = \rho/\sinh\rho$, which with $\rho$ taken as a radius is the field of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield monopole of flat space, a result Chamseddine and Volkov called "quite surprising" [chamseddine1997]. The space has the topology of $\mathbb{R}^4$, and the other solutions are singular at the centre, among them the one with $w = 0$, the field of a Dirac monopole [chamseddine1997, chamseddine1998].¶Far from the centre all curvature invariants tend to zero, but not fast enough for the space to be asymptotically flat, and no total energy can be assigned to it [chamseddine1997]. The plane of $t$ and $\rho$ is conformal to half of the flat plane, so the conformal diagram is that of Minkowski space, and the spacetime is geodesically complete and globally hyperbolic [chamseddine1997]. The negative cosmological term focuses timelike geodesics, which oscillate about the centre, each with its own period, so that geodesics leaving one event do not meet again [chamseddine1997]. In Schwarzschild coordinates, known only parametrically through $r = a\sqrt{R\sinh\rho}$, the amplitude $w$ falls off as a power of $r$, since every field of the theory is massless [chamseddine1998].¶Chamseddine and Volkov also obtained the gauged theory from supergravity in ten dimensions on a group manifold, and with it lifted the monopole to a solution of string theory at leading order [chamseddine1998]. In the string frame the lift near the centre is Minkowski space of seven dimensions times a 3-sphere, and the Yang-Mills field appears as components off the diagonal of the metric [chamseddine1998]. Juan Maldacena and Carlos Nuñez found that the lift is the geometry of a large number of fivebranes wrapped on a 2-sphere, whose theory at low energy is pure $N = 1$ super Yang-Mills [maldacena2001]. They took the solution from Chamseddine and Volkov and showed that it is smooth and that the gauge theory dual to it confines [maldacena2001]. Worldsheet instantons break the chiral symmetry $U(1)_R$ of that theory to $Z_{2N}$, and the solution breaks it further to $Z_2$, with $N$ different solutions for its $N$ vacua [maldacena2001]. The Abelian solution with the field of a Dirac monopole is singular at its centre, and Maldacena and Nuñez compared the two as an SU(2) monopole compares with a Dirac monopole [maldacena2001].¶Steven S. Gubser, Arkady A. Tseytlin, and Volkov showed in 2001 that the supersymmetric solutions form a single family with the monopole as its only regular member, and found black holes with regular horizons in the same theory [gubser2001nonabelian]. None of those black holes is colder than the Hagedorn temperature of the little string theory on the fivebranes, and their entropy falls as their temperature rises [gubser2001nonabelian]. Diego H. Correa, Enrique F. Moreno, Sebastien Reuillon, and Fidel A. Schaposnik took the Penrose limit along a radial null geodesic in 2003, which needed the gauge coupling scaled to zero, and found a plane wave keeping twice the monopole's supersymmetries [correa2003]. Chamseddine and Volkov placed the monopole in 2004 inside an $N = 4$ supergravity with gauge group $SO(4)$, where a ratio $\xi$ of two gauge couplings deforms it, for $\xi > 0$, into spaces that approach anti-de Sitter space "with an excess of the solid angle" [chamseddine2004]. At $\xi = 1$ the deformed solution is anti-de Sitter space, and for $\xi < 0$ its spatial sections have the topology of a 3-sphere [chamseddine2004].¶Burkhard Kleihaus, Jutta Kunz, and Eugen Radu found in 2008 an exact solution for the monopole in a background magnetic field, and it reduces to the monopole when the field is switched off [kleihaus2008]. Chamseddine and Volkov found in 2011 an infinite tower of bound states among the small perturbations of the monopole, with the same frequencies for bosons of either parity and for fermions [chamseddine2011]. A fermion scattered off the monopole flips its isospin, as fermions scattered off a monopole of flat space do [chamseddine2011]. Fabio Podestà and Alberto Raffero proved in 2026 that a family of complete metrics on the affine quadric, a space of six dimensions, joins a Ricci-flat Kähler metric to the metric of six dimensions in the lift [podesta2026]. Every member of their family other than the Kähler one has positive scalar curvature [podesta2026].

related.text: Another static ball of Yang-Mills field held by gravity with no Higgs field. It is not supersymmetric and has no magnetic charge [chamseddine1997].

The magnetic black hole of the same supergravity with both gauge couplings set to zero, an Abelian field, and a dilaton. In that theory the static, spherically symmetric, purely magnetic supersymmetric solutions are these black holes [chamseddine1998].

A monopole of scalar fields whose spheres far from the centre have less area than in flat space at the same distance. Here the spheres have more, and in Schwarzschild coordinates, with $g_{rr} = 1/N$, the function $N$ grows as $\ln r$ [chamseddine1997].

Another monopole that is a regular geometry in more dimensions, a vacuum solution in five. Lifted to ten dimensions, the Yang-Mills field of this monopole also appears in the metric, as components mixing the four dimensions with a 3-sphere [chamseddine1998].

The string frame of fivebranes in flat space has a dilaton linear in the distance down their throat. Far from the centre the lift of this monopole to ten dimensions has a dilaton linear in its radial coordinate as well, with a logarithmic correction [maldacena2001].

In the SO(4) gauged supergravity a ratio $\xi$ of two gauge couplings deforms the monopole into spaces that approach anti-de Sitter space with an excess of solid angle, and at $\xi = 1$ into anti-de Sitter space [chamseddine2004].
The plane of $t$ and $\rho$ is conformal to half of the flat plane, so the monopole has the conformal diagram of Minkowski space, although its curvature does not vanish [chamseddine1997].

coordinates.name: Chamseddine-Volkov

parameters.description: Scale of the monopole, a length, which the field equations leave free: the metric and $e^{2\phi}$ grow as $a^2$
Dimensionless, with $R^2 = \rho^2 + O(\rho^4)$ near the centre and $R^2 = 2\rho + O(1)$ far away; the sphere at $\rho$ has the areal radius $r = a\sqrt{R\sinh\rho}$

coordinates.convention: We use Chamseddine and Volkov's coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \varphi)$ [chamseddine1997], with $t$ and $\rho$ dimensionless, so $t$ is itself the chart's $x^0$. The Yang-Mills field has the amplitude $w = \rho/\sinh\rho$ and the dilaton is $e^{2\phi} = a^2\sinh\rho/(2R)$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
